articles.text: Bond for new pool to be on ballot Nov. 3 Piedmont Community Pool After a lengthy discussion at a July 6 meeting, the Piedmont City Council directed the city staff to prepare documents to place a general obligation bond on the ballot on November 3, 2020 that would create a new Piedmont Community Pool. The decision follows a series of discussions in the past four years and was a more detailed discussion of the pool’s fate at a June 29 meeting. At that meeting, more than 100 community members participated in a virtual meeting on Zoom, and at least 30 residents voiced their opinion. A majority of those residents were in favor of having a community pool, either by restoring the current facility or creating a new one. The council will move forward with a possible bond to appear on the November 2020 ballot. The estimated bond amount is currently $15 million, but staff is waiting on updated cost estimates for the conceptual master plan adopted in November 2016. A conceptual master plan went through a rigorous community process four years ago, and an operational analysis proved that it was favorable. “[When] taking inf lation into account, the city is engaging a consultant to evaluate on a number that feels realistic. There is always some risk for the unknowns, but a solid number will be given before a first reading on this item,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. Details on cost estimates will be presented to council on July 20. Residents poured in during public comment on Monday to show support of a new pool facility, and a subsequent bond to fund it in November. Steve Collins, President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO), said that the organization would support enhancing the city’s aquatic facilities.

articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on June 30. Thank you for your tireless dedication to the city. We have been fortunate that 56 years ago, a group of visionary citizens saw fit to raise funding to enable this city to have a public pool. After having heard the eloquent pleas from the city’s young people, I hope that one of the take-aways you gleaned is that the pool has a broad base of support across ages because it is an affordable public asset that reflects Piedmont’s inclusive civic values. As last night’s speakers pointed out, the pool supports physical and mental health & well-being for young and old, including learn-to-swim for the very young, aquatic sports & exercise for students, special education, and adults. As a number of the young people pointed out, not everyone in Piedmont can afford to join a private club with a pool. The pool’s broad public benefit justifies an ongoing subsidy. As Jon Sakol pointed out, the outside consultant hired by the city had expressed that the level of subsidy the city has had to incur to date is, on average, within the range, if not slightly lower, compared to other city pools. Consequently, as you consider whether or not to re-open the pool in the near term and the longer term ballot measure for a bond to finance a new pool, I urge you to adopt a frame of mind along the lines of “how best to maintain a pool in Piedmont” versus one of “whether to have a pool in Piedmont”. To that end, in the interests of preserving this important inclusive cultural legacy, I urge you to propose a ballot measure that combines the pool with other infrastructure projects so that voters can choose to invest in preserving our infrastructure that benefits a broad cross section of our community as a package. -Jackie Khor Liu For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: And so the MAGA magical thinking tour continues, driven by the engine of denial and delusion, the rhetorical umbrella remains that Covid-19 will “go away without a vaccine.” No matter that as of this writing, 2.5 million people in the U.S. have been infected, 126,494 people have died, and 29 states are today reporting new highs in reported cases. The reality is haunting, deadly and ignored. Our shambolic pandemic policy continues to be shaped by a needy, ego-driven president who refuses to wear the totemic mask, now appearing to be a surreal symbol of conservative defiance and a statement of personal freedom. And there are, of course, the virus denying, maskless MAGA rallies, such as those recently held in Tulsa and Phoenix, where, from the podium, Trump voiced his rejection of testing (fewer tests, fewer cases to, “slow the testing down”), committing once again political malfeasance on an extraordinary level, and his rejection of science simply breathtaking. Meanwhile the culture wars continue, and the defense of Confederate statuary leads while hospitalizations rise and the ICUs once again begin to fill and the white noise of ventilators surrounds gown shrouded family members, standing in stark hospital rooms, pleading to say goodbye. But as we move into the heart of summer, I find that I also worry that the tone of desperation and incoherence revealed by Trump in the Tulsa and Phoenix speeches were but precursors to what awaits us in the months ahead as the campaign heats up.

Beninati and Bowers were introduced by LWV Bowers spoke about police reform within the Piedmont Police Department, touching on changes made well before the killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis and subsequent protests. Bowers said there is a small number of African Americans in leadership roles in police departments across California and referenced the progress his own department has made on the “Eight Can’t Wait” suggested reforms. The Eight Can’t Wait campaign offers eight immediate steps that organizers say could make a major dent in the amount of police violence, or the unnecessary killing of civilians. The plan calls on departments across the country to ban chokeholds and strangleholds, require de-escalation strategies, require warnings before shooting, exhaust all alternatives before shooting, ban shooting at moving vehicles, require use of force continuum and comprehensive reporting, and require officers to intervene when they see inappropriate use The Piedmont Police Department has banned the use of the Carotid Control Hold. A pointby-point response to each tenet of the Eight Can’t Wait campaign is available on the Piedmont Police Department’s website. Though most of these changes were made prior to the killing of George Floyd, Bowers said there is still work to be done in respect to “We’ve instituted policy changes, but we’re continuing to look internally,” Bowers said. He also addressed calls from civilians to defund police depart- –CA Deputy Attorney General Nancy Beninati. Perspective from State Beninati described her two decades of work on the intersection of police practices and civil rights and focused on bias statistic and the Racial and Identity Profiling Act of 2015. In the last five years, she has focused on constitutional police reform through investigations and collaborative reform. Beninati has also flagged other departments for taking too long to reform. Earlier this year in a report to San Francisco Police Chief Bill Scott, she wrote that “California Department of Justice is concerned that SFPD’s progress is too slow. Beninati discussed actions that civilians can take to ensure a more just and equitable community. “I urge everyone to hold their [police] chiefs accountable. Attend community meetings, go to your department’s website and make suggestions for improvement,” she said. Beninati also suggested that community members demand transparency by obtaining public records and file a citizen complaint if you believe you were unfairly treated. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will hold its General Municipal Election on November 3, 2020. The nomination period for two vacancies on the Piedmont City Council and three vacancies on the Board of Education opens on Monday, July 13. The deadline for submitting completed paperwork is Friday, August 7 at 5:00 p.m. There is no cost to file for election. The City Council and Board of Education are Piedmont’s two elected bodies and guide the operation of City government and the Piedmont Unified School District respectively. Members of these bodies may serve a maximum of two consecutive four-year terms. The City publishes the Guide to Nomination and Candidacy, which provides details about the nomination and candidacy process which prospective candidates should find useful. This election will take place in the context of the COVID- 19 pandemic. While there have been some changes to election procedures on a statewide scale to provide for social distancing, many of the steps in getting a candidate’s name on the ballot involve person to person contact. Among other requirements, candidates must turn in at least twenty, but no more than thirty valid signatures to have their name placed on the ballot. The Alameda County Health Officer’s Shelter in Place Order specifically defines signature gathering as an essential government function, which is allowed under the order. The California Elections Code requires that nomination papers be issued in person to the prospective candidate at City Hall. Because many city staff are working at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic, prospective candidates are required to schedule an appointment to take out nomination papers with the City Clerk’s office. An appointment will also be required to submit the nomination papers once the candidate has completed their work. These appointments generally last between 30 minutes and one hour. Residents with questions about the process or wishing to make an appointment can call the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040 or send an email to cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov.

Beninati is also the former LWVP president. The discussion, held via teleconference application Zoom, was followed by a question and answer session. Beninati and Bowers were introduced by LWV member Lois Corrin. Bowers spoke about police reform within the Piedmont Police Department, touching on changes made well before the killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis and subsequent protests. Bowers said there is a small number of African Americans in leadership roles in police departments across California and referenced the progress his own department has made on the “Eight Can’t Wait” suggested reforms. The Eight Can’t Wait campaign offers eight immediate steps that organizers say could make a major dent in the amount of police violence, or the unnecessary killing of civilians. The plan calls on departments across the country to ban chokeholds and strangleholds, require de-escalation strategies, require warnings before shooting, exhaust all alternatives before shooting, ban shooting at moving vehicles, require use of force continuum and comprehensive reporting, and require officers to intervene when they see inappropriate use of force. The Piedmont Police Department has banned the use of the Carotid Control Hold. A pointby-point response to each tenet of the Eight Can’t Wait campaign is available on the Piedmont Police Department’s website. Though most of these changes were made prior to the killing of George Floyd, Bowers said there is still work to be done in respect to overall police reform. “We’ve instituted policy changes, but we’re continuing to look internally,” Bowers said. He also addressed calls from civilians to defund police depart- “I urge everyone to hold their [police] chiefs accountable.” –CA Deputy Attorney General Nancy Beninati. Piedmont’s Park Commission was asked to consider a recommendation to City Council to install electric vehicle charging stations in the city. Commission members unanimously approved the recommendation, and the proposal will be considered at a City Council meeting in the near future. Due to costs and other criteria, the city has been ineligible for grants from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District for the installation of public electric vehicle chargers. The new proposal would provide five chargers with a total of nine charging ports, at no cost to the city. The charging stations would be owned, operated and maintained by East Bay Community Energy, which services electricity to Piedmont. Piedmont Climate Action Fellow Justin Szasz introduced the proposal to the commissioners at a July 1 meeting, held via Zoom. The proposal would place electric vehicle chargers on streetlights in Piedmont. These would be “Level 2” chargers, which would charge vehicles for 10 to 20 miles of range an hour. A second proposal would include “DC fast kiosk chargers,” which can charge an electric vehicle for 360 miles of range in an hour. That proposal includes the Community Hall and Ace Hardware locations. Suggested locations for chargers are near Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue, in the parking lot at the Community Center, and on Highland and Craig Avenue next to Havens School. But the city’s failure to provide advance notice of the project drew criticism from some. “I am writing to urge the Park Commission not to approve the EV Charging Station Proposal at its meeting later today. The total lack of time for public input on this proposal is egregious. The notice is dated June 26, just last Friday. I have seen no news of this proposal, either in the Post or the Exedra. That is not surprising since there has not been time for either news source to publish news of its existence,” resident Cameron Wolfe said. Each charging port would be next to a parking space, which would be reserved specifically for electric vehicles. The price would be competitive with other electric chargers and would be less expensive than gas for non-electric cars. “It is staff’s belief that this program may help to meet the general plan and climate action plan goals in emission reduction,” Szasz said.

articles.text: Piedmont High School head tennis coach Jim Landis made the start of summer official. He began operating tennis clinics last week, and suddenly the courts at the Corey Reich Tennis Center came to life. To abide by the Alameda County’s restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic, all participants were wearing masks, and the groups, now called pods, were limited to 12 kids at a time and instructors stayed with their pod for three weeks. During each hour and half session, campers have several water breaks during which everyone is required to use hand sanitizer. Landis confirmed that quite a few parents stayed to watch on Monday, the first day, to see how the camp would operate during the coronavirus. He received few concerns from parents. The tennis clinic, running from Monday to Friday each week has three sessions each day based upon age. Campers from age 8-12 are in the first group, players 13-18 are in the second group, and advanced players comprise the final group. In total, there are 60 players throughout the day, similar to prior years. The difference in 2020 is that there are more instructors, creating a four to one player to instructor ratio. Current restrictions in Alameda County require that instructors not be in more than one pod of campers.

articles.text: Quarantine is boring, no doubt about that, but if you’re bored you can always try work. Last week, I remodeled my room because I needed to do something with my hands and give myself a change of scenery. The project took me about a week and gave me something to do and something to look forward to. I started by going to Ace Hardware to get painting supplies (you’ll need brushes, trays, drop clothes, tarp to cover your furniture and spackle to cover up holes in your walls.) And as soon as I walked in, I was out of my element and walked around completely lost. The store was packed, which made my navigation even harder. Eventually I got to the paint section and asked a very kind worker to point me in the right direction for all my supplies. There I chose the three colors that I wanted – blue, yellow and grey. I got samples and took them home, put them on my wall and looked at them until I knew which one I liked the best. ( I chose blue.) The following day I went back to Ace to get the remaining supplies and the buckets of paint. The next few days were chaotic. We had to move all of my furniture out of my room and that took a long time. My dad had to step off some of his calls and help me put primer on my walls (that’s basically like white paint to block out the old color – purple in my case). That took four hours and it smelled horrible, and when I say horrible, I mean worse than locker room horrible. After the primer dried overnight, I got my sister and my dad to help me paint. Then we let the walls dry and moved the furniture back in, but not all of it. It seemed like a good time to unclutter the room. Not everyone was happy; my mom had to find a place for the stuff I didn’t want back. The whole project took about a week, but it was well worth it because now my room finally looks aesthetically pleasing. The hardest thing about room remodeling is not figuring out what color you want; it’s securing your family’s support. Some members might not be that excited about adding remodel to the quarantine. My dad was supportive, and my sister was a mix of seven different emotions. Personally, I was very confident with the decision to re-paint my room, even when my mother said that the blue color I’d chosen looked like a hospital room color, the yellow too much like the kitchen, and the grey was depressing. But in the end, everybody, even Mom, was happy. As a first-time painter I learned that there are a lot of do’s and don’ts.

articles.text: County reopening plans put on pause A new case of COVID-19 was confirmed in Piedmont on Friday, July 3. As the global pandemic continues into July, Piedmont’s surrounding area has been much harder hit by COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus. Cases across Alameda County increased to 6,887 by Monday, July 6, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Tragically, another five people have died of the disease since June 23, increasing the number of total fatalities in Alameda County to 140. Alameda County continues to be the hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter in the region, now counts 5,478 cases and 165 total deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 4,020 and there have been 50 deaths. In total, there have been 14 cases reported in Piedmont. 10 were reported before April 13 and three during May. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, 2,712 cases were reported. Hayward now has a total of 1,116. Fremont has reported 362 cases and San Leandro has also reported 345. Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials on Monday, June 29 as concerns mount about COVID-19 hospitalizations. The new order does not reverse previous reopening orders, but the county is now postponing its plan to phase in the next stage of reopening, which would allow for indoor dining, salons, barbershops, pools and professional sports, although without the presence of fans. An order that went into place on June 19 allowed for outdoor museums, outdoor restaurant dining, some religious services, indoor retail, mall shopping and outdoor fitness classes. On Thursday, July 2, county officials urged residents to stay home during the Independence Day holiday. “We can all help protect our families, friends and neighbors by celebrating the Fourth of July at home this year,” wrote Dr. Nicholas Moss, who is taking over for Dr. Erica Pan as the Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Cases and hospitalizations are rising across the region and COVID-19 spreads most easily when people who don’t live together gather in groups.” In Piedmont, the City’s annual Fourth of July Parade was canceled, although a socially distant, front yard decoration celebration took place. While the county had been opening up new sectors of the economy about every two weeks through June, that process has been paused for the time being. The department said that last week and this week will be critical for assessing how to reopen more activities. Statewide, 271,684 COVID-19 cases were reported as of Sunday, July 5, an increase of over 55,000 in a week. In California, 6,337 people have died since the outbreak began. Last week, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that 19 counties were on a “watchlist” and must close down many indoor businesses and restaurants. He added four counties to the list on Monday, July 6, including Marin County. Contra Costa and Solano Counties were also on the watchlist. Alameda County is not on this watchlist, but at a City Council meeting this week, Piedmont officials said it was likely that the county will be added to the list in the future. In a notice from June, Piedmont noted that Alameda County’s face covering requirements are still in effect – face coverings must be work at all times in public, even if a person is exercising. Face coverings can only be removed if a person will not be within 30 feet of another person from outside the household. The City of Piedmont keeps all of its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19

Mothers Trail provides a 1,000-foot climb in one-mile to Moses Rock Ridge. Staff Photos Last week we headed to Mt. Diablo’s Burma Road: a climb of 2,000 feet to Moses Rock Ridge. Burma Road to the Moses Rock Ridge is an out-and-back 3.1 miles hike. Your trail starts on North Gate Road, which is already an epic understatement itself. Be prepared to climb at a rate of 1,000 feet per mile. There were times I was walking purely on my toes given the steep grade of Burma Road. The hike starts with a bang, requiring you to ascend 530 feet in just a half mile, followed by an easier 230 feet climb in 0.4 of a mile to your first junction. But any ease will quickly be forgotten after turning left onto Mothers Trail. A tenth of amile in you’ll turn right and into your final ascent to the top, gaining some 550 feet in elevation within the next half mile to the next junction. Prior to turning right to continue on Burma Road, you’ll pass a man-made watering hole, presumably left for cattle that used to graze the fields. Etched into the round concrete walls of the miniature pond is “Burma Springs, 1968. A school of koi fish swam undisturbed in the remote hillside location. After the junction, you’ll climb another 500 feet in one mile to the Moses Rock Ridge and Deer Flat Road junction. Continuing down Deer Flat Road for another half mile will add 400 more feet of elevation and close out the 3.1 mile trek to the Diablo Valley Overlook, which provides a sweeping view of Contra Costa County, Diablo Valley, and all the way to Suisun Bay. Throughout your trail, your view gets more magnificent by the step. With each rest after ascents, the view of the rolling foothills of Mt. Diablo from the Moses Rock Ridge trail. short moments. With just a few groves of treecover along the hike, bring sunblock and other sun-protective gear. The inland Contra Costa heat may take a toll, especially on the steep trails, so be sure to arrive early. Despite Mt. Diablo’s popularity, there were no other hikers on my entire trek. Given Mt. Diablo has a population of mountain lions and rattlesnakes, bringing a friend may be wise. Keep in mind that rattlers enjoy resting on trails during the summer months. Being wary of your surroundings is imperative on lesser-known back country hikes like this. articles.text: Alex Weekes, PHS Class of 2020, is working out at Team Prep USA’s summer running camp in Colorado. A senior leader from the upcoming Piedmont High class of 2021, Alex Weekes, is eying a big campaign for the end of his high school career. Currently in Colorado at the Team Prep USA camp, he is using the altitude to his advantage. “We were in Boulder one week, which is around 5,000 feet in elevation. Now, I’m in Gunnison around 7,700 feet, so it feels a lot different. We’re doing a lot of runs up to 9,000-10,000 feet. I’ve been here for a while, but I’m still getting used to this elevation,” explained Weekes. It marks his second summer program at Team Prep USA. The camp has hosted former Olympic champions like 3000-meter steeplechase winner Emma Coburn. Former Piedmont Post 2018 Athlete of the Year Reece Proctor is also a former attendee. “I came to the camp last year and really enjoyed my experience, so I wanted to return this summer,” said Weekes. “We’re focusing on two longer runs throughout the four-week course, and we’re doing a lot of base training. Every run is on a dirt road or on trail-type courses, but the elevation really makes a difference,” he added. “It’s among the only overnight summer camps that is happening this year. We have to follow a lot of protocols, like wearing masks when not running or eating and social-distance from people not within your pod of 10 runners,” he said. Last year Weekes emerged as a team leader and was named to the second-team All-League after finishing 10th of 74 at the WACC Championship meet in 16:31. “By the end of last season, we saw we had a chance to qualify for State but didn’t make it. It seemed to light a fire under everybody,” said Weekes, noting that Piedmont finished 5th of 22 team at the North Coast Section championship and failed by two places to advance to the State meet. Weekes will be joining a group of upperclassmen, including firstteam recipient and classmate Collin Mortimer, who finished fifth at the league finals. Rowen Connelly is another senior, and according to PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund is running 30 miles weekly. He clocked a 16:48.9 at the league championship, finishing 18th. Juniors Seamus Chamberlain Carr and Cooper Downing are were two more runners to frequently finish as the boys’ topfive group. “We really started to believe as the year went on. We have a strong five already right there. If we have a season, we have the potential to do very well. We have the mindset going in this time,” said Weekes. With the close of the spring track season and powering through an offseason program unlike any other, Weeks says he’s just looking forward to seeing some familiar faces again. “With losing the spring track season, it was a strange way to walk away. I’m definitely excited to get back, talk to friends, and see how they’re doing,” added Weekes. As for the standing of fall sports, the CIF is expected to make an announcement on July 20. The NFHS has regarded running sports as a “low risk” transmission, so there is some optimism toward a cross country schedule.

articles.text: The 2003 girls’ team won the school’s only North Coast Section championship in soccer. With the Premier League and European soccer as the marquee sport during the worldwide pandemic, we take a look back at Piedmont High’s only North Coast Section soccer championship – the girls’ team in 2003. In 2003 Giants’ legend Barry Bonds won the third of four consecutive Most Valuable Player awards. Cristiano Ronaldo made his Manchester United debut at age 18. In Piedmont, it was year of history. Twins Courtney and Ashley Paris led the basketball team to the school’s first state championship in any sport, then repeated it in 2004. With a group of friends who had played and competed together for seven years, the girls’ soccer team won the NCS championship ­ also a first in school history. They remain the only Piedmont High soccer team – boys or girls – to win a section title. Their team finished with a school-record 24-1-1 overall record and a Bay Shore Athletic League championship, securing the top-seed in the 2A playoffs. But they never had it easy in the playoffs, defeating No. 8 El Cerrito 4-1 but requiring a win by penalty kicks against No. 5 Las Lomas in the semifinals. In the championship game, Piedmont faced crosstown rivals Bishop O’Dowd, then the lead team in the Hayward Area Athletic League. After regulation, the game was still scoreless at 0-0. In penalty kicks, Catherine Betts scored the game-winner in sudden death overtime. That year’s team featured two athletes signing with Division 1 programs: Whitney Temple to Loyola Marymount and Catherine Betts to Oregon State. Temple was a four-year starter at Piedmont and led them in scoring during that time. She was a three-year starter at LMU and team captain. “As a freshman, Temple became an equal scoring threat on Piedmont’s team with Liz Dosa [who went on to play at Michigan]. In four years, Temple helped lead the Highlanders to four league championships and two appearances in the semifinals of the North Coast Section championships,” wrote Post editor Gray Cathrall in 2003. Betts played for Oregon State and eventually transferred to the University of the Pacific. At the time she told the Post that she wanted to pursue a career in sports therapy and seemingly has pursued that dream. Betts, who briefly returned to Piedmont as an assistant coach for the girls’ team in 2009-2010, became health and performance coach and launched Betts Fit LLC, which patented an innovative sports bra design. Whitney Temple, Class of 2003, was a four-year starter at Piedmont and played college soccer at Loyola Marymount. Catherine Betts, Class of 2003, went on to play for Oregon State and UOP before starting a career in sports sciences.

articles.text: A map of the 2020 Tour de France, which starts on August 29. The 107th edition of the Tour de France is set to begin after being rescheduled from August 29 in Nice to September 20 in Paris after COVID-19 forced the tour to reschedule from June 27. The Tour anticipates a course that starts with the 2020 Grand Départ from Nice; a 170 km ride into France’s Var Valley to Sisteron. Stage 2 climbs 187 km to the Nice Haut Pays with nearly 4,000 meters of ascent. Another critical point will be the back-to-back mountain courses of Stage 8 and 9, which are respective 140 km and 154 km courses. Like the first mountain stage, Stage 8 will include three cols (mountain passes) and require more than 4,000 meters of elevation gain for cyclists. Stage 9 has one steep ascent up Cole de la Hourcere at 1,440 meters. From there, Stages 16, 17, and 18 are three consecutive mountain stages and could certainly form the eventual Yellow Jersey winner. Stage 16 goes 164 km from La Tour de Pin to Villard de Lans; Stage 17 travels 168 km from Grenoble to Col de la Loze; and 18 goes another 168 km from Méribel to La Roche-sur-Foro. But before the official Grand Boucle, the tour is hosting online virtual unofficial session using Zwift until July 19—a homebased interactive video game where contestants use their bike on a stand. The big trio from Team INEOS in competing in the virtual event, including 2019 Tour winner Egan Bernal, 2018 winner Geraint Thomas, and 2017 Chris Froome, who won in 2013, 2015, and 2016 as well. Other elite men’s riders include Julian Alaphilippe, Greg Van Avermaet, Mathieu van der Poel, Nairo Quintana, Mads Pedersen, and Romain Bardet. articles.text: Shotgun Players’ Kill the Debbie Downers is an adaptation of Chekhov’s 1901 play, Three Sisters. Shotgun Players is offering past performances on its website throughout the current health crisis. This week, patrons can view Kill the Debbie Downers, Kill Them, Kill Them, Kill Them Off, a theater piece inspired by Anton Chekhov’s Three Sisters. Checkhov wrote Three Sisters in 1901, four years before an attempted revolution in Russia. “One can already feel that revolution on the horizon in Three Sisters, its rumble of change exciting and unnerving the characters. And yet as in a Beckett play ‘they do not move.’ What revolutions are rumbling on our horizon?” read the program notes. The cast includes Nathaniel Andalis, Gabby Battista, Amanda Farbstein, Sam Jackson, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart, and Billy Raphael. The cast of six switches roles throughout the production. The play is directed by Mark Jackson and Beth Wilmurt, and was originally performed in March and April last year. The video has been made available through the Shotgun Players’ website for patrons to enjoy during shelter-in-place regulations. You can watch the full play on Youtube at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=-nUmgLJXSGU&- feature=youtu.be. The play is approximately 120 minutes. Erin Mei-Ling Stuart plays Masha.

Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field, a consummate actress, creates a person who, while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues), is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood living in a van; she is also in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. To add to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of unread magazines decades old). Her packrat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology; rather, like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train long ago has left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it and now, suddenly, has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Starring Sally Field, Max Greenfield and Tyne Daly. Directed by Michael Showalter. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on April 27, 2016. Sally Field stars in a scene from Hello, My Name is Doris. Movie review by Chris Honoré I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that, while eccentric, was also deeply human. This was a substantive part. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. Doris sits alone, grieving; the deceased is her mother, whose profile is barely visible in the coffin. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with bric-a-brac. Now in her 60s, Doris works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry. Despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves – she remains, to most of her young co-workers, essentially invisible. Seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise and touches her to the core. She is awakened, consumed by feelings that cause her to all but levitate, as if she had been this loose string on a violin that is now taut and vibrates as she begins to have these Walter Mitty moments where John is concerned. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, and allows herself to believe that what he sees is the Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name is Doris. Dev Patel & Rooney Mara in a scene from Lion. Movie review by Chris Honoré The challenge inherent in reviewing a splendid film such as Lion is how to offer the reader a sense of the film without depriving viewers of experiencing the story, one fresh reveal after the next. Perhaps the only aspects of the story that should be disclosed are those shown in the trailer, three minutes that give just enough information to frame what will be a life changing event in a small boy’s life. Five-year old Saroo is played by newcomer Sunny Pawar, who gives a spectacular performance. His mother is a laborer in a rock quarry in Khandwa, India. He and his older brother, Guddu (Abhishek Bharate), scramble each day to supplement the family’s small income, often stealing coal from passing trains. Poverty defines the family, but the boys are resilient and deeply close. One night, Guddu is going out to find anything he can sell or trade and tells Saroo to stay at home. Saroo begs to go along and finally Guddu relents. At a local train station, Saroo is sleepy, exhausted, and Guddu leaves him on a bench, telling him not to wait for him. Saroo promises and immediately falls asleep. When he wakes, some hours later, the station is empty and all is quiet. He calls out for Guddu but hears only silence. He wanders over to an empty train waiting trackside and makes the fateful decision to go on board. Finding a softer seat than the station bench, he again falls asleep. When he wakes it is daylight and the train is moving, the countryside flashing by. Nicole Kidman and Sunny Pawar star in Lion.

The train does not stop until it reaches a station in Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), and massive numbers of people, waiting on the platform, begin to board. Saroo pushes his way off the train, looking around for anything familiar. What he is unaware of is that he is 1,000 miles away from home and at a complete loss as how to get back. And he doesn’t know where back is. He is suddenly alone. Lost. Endless crowds of people move around him, ignoring him, like a small rock in a rushing stream. This long first act is gripping, breathtaking, filled with heartfelt tension. How will small Saroo ever survive on the urban mean streets where predatory adults victimize abandoned children. And so begins a brief act two, which leads into act three and we meet a grown Saroo (Dev Patel) whose life has been completely changed forever. But this older Saroo who once was lost now must be found. Be prepared to be caught up in this wonderful film. It will touch you as you absorb not only little Saroo’s circumstances, but as you later engage with him as a young man. Not incidentally, Both Dev Patel and Nicole Kidman were nominated for Golden Globes for their very fine performances. Lion. Starring Dev Patel, Sunny Pawar, Rooney Mara and Nicole Kidman. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with bric-a-brac. Now in her 60s, Doris works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry. Despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves – she remains, to most of her young co-workers, essentially invisible. Seen but not seen. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise and touches her to the core. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, and allows herself to believe that what he sees is the Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name is Doris. Movie review by Chris Honoré The challenge inherent in reviewing a splendid film such as Lion is how to offer the reader a sense of the film without depriving viewers of experiencing the story, one fresh reveal after the next. Perhaps the only aspects of the story that should be disclosed are those shown in the trailer, three minutes that give just enough information to frame what will be a life changing event in a small boy’s life. Five-year old Saroo is played by newcomer Sunny Pawar, who gives a spectacular performance. His mother is a laborer in a rock quarry in Khandwa, India. He and his older brother, Guddu (Abhishek Bharate), scramble each day to supplement the family’s small income, often stealing coal from passing trains. Poverty defines the family, but the boys are resilient and deeply close. One night, Guddu is going out to find anything he can sell or trade and tells Saroo to stay at home. Saroo begs to go along and finally Guddu relents. At a local train station, Saroo is sleepy, exhausted, and Guddu leaves him on a bench, telling him not to wait for him. Saroo promises and immediately falls asleep. When he wakes, some hours later, the station is empty and all is quiet. He calls out for Guddu but hears only silence. He wanders over to an empty train waiting trackside and makes the fateful decision to go on board. Finding a softer seat than the station bench, he again falls asleep. When he wakes it is daylight and the train is moving, the countryside flashing by. He runs up and down the vacant aisles, calling out for Guddu… for anyone. The train does not stop until it reaches a station in Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), and massive numbers of people, waiting on the platform, begin to board. Saroo pushes his way off the train, looking around for anything familiar. What he is unaware of is that he is 1,000 miles away from home and at a complete loss as how to get back. And he doesn’t know where back is. He is suddenly alone. Lost. Endless crowds of people move around him, ignoring him, like a small rock in a rushing stream. This long first act is gripping, breathtaking, filled with heartfelt tension. How will small Saroo ever survive on the urban mean streets where predatory adults victimize abandoned children. And so begins a brief act two, which leads into act three and we meet a grown Saroo (Dev Patel) whose life has been completely changed forever. But this older Saroo who once was lost now must be found. Be prepared to be caught up in this wonderful film. It will touch you as you absorb not only little Saroo’s circumstances, but as you later engage with him as a young man. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré For all of its CGI-animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creator of the Toy Story franchise, has never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Saoirse Ronan and Eliza Scanlen in a scene from Little Women. Movie review by Chris Honoré All fiction, however thin the thread, inevitably is autobiographical. The writer’s persona, in some way, reveals itself. And so it is with Louisa May Alcott’s iconic 19th century novel, Little Women, in which the central character, Jo March (Saoirse Ronan), is unabashedly Alcott. It should not be a surprise that writer/director Greta Gerwig would place Jo’s writing, first her short pieces and plays, and then the creation of her book, at the center of what proves to be a remarkable adaptation of this resilient and timeless story. Of course, the contrasts between the 1860s and today are stark; yet, there is a prescient, rebellious modernity to Little Women that is inescapable. The world of women then was defined by norms that, in the main, rendered them powerless. There was an absence of civil rights, including, and they were bound and diminished by an insidious inequality. The way forward for most women, especially those of little means, was a path of narrow options, most often limited to marriage and motherhood. And yet, in this milieu of such cultural expectations, Gerwig focuses on Jo, one of four sisters – Meg (Emma Watson), Amy (Florence Pugh), Beth (Eliza Scanlen), and their mother, Marmee (Lora Dern). It is Jo who is headstrong, intent on becoming a writer, her dresser drawer filled with plays and stories, a young woman fiercely independent, often finding herself at odds with the reactions by others to her abrasive, outspoken points of view. It is Jo’s intention to be a person apart. She declares emphatically that she will never marry and will make her way financially with her pen. Above all, as she insists defiantly, she will row her own canoe. And yet – and this is a tender, complex and powerful contradiction with which Jo struggles – she realizes that she thrives in the loving embrace of her family. Jo wants above all for the March family – this warm, eruptive, loving group of women – to remain as it is, as it has always been, and wills it never to change. In one scene, on the eve of Meg’s wedding, she pleads with her sister not to marry, arguing that in two years she will have grown tired of all of it. Better to remain at home, no matter that she, Jo, will make her own journey to New York to work as a tutor while submitting her stories to a local publisher. As writer and director Gerwig takes risks, not only in her creative interpretation of the novel, but in constructing a narrative that bifurcates the film, moving from the early years of the March sisters to that period when they are adults. Into that mix she adds dream-like scenes that focus on alternative outcomes that are unrealized, implying that in Jo, when reacting to the realities of life, we do not always have a reliable narrator. It’s an aspect of the film that enhances and never detracts, for it reveals the tension between what is and what should be, if only life were fair. Little Women is also nimbly and wonderfully filled with moments that resonate because of their humanity and their inherent decency. Jo looks out a window, and watches her sister Meg and her husband, John (James Norton), touchingly embrace. Jo and Beth rest side by side on a windswept beach, lost in conversation (a foreshadowing of what lies ahead for Beth). And there are the steely, sororal bonds made manifest, their history inextricably binding them together, this band of young sisters. G e r w ig, u nexp e ct e d ly, includes a scene when Jo looks into the camera and speaks to an empty room while not breaking the fourth wall (a film, like a play, has, typically, only three dimensions); rather she lets her thoughts become concrete sounds, words to be weighed and considered, ripe for reflection. It’s audacious but effective. Little Women is a beautifully made film, superbly acted. It is Gerwig’s best work to date. As well, perhaps it’s an antidote to our driven, cynical times; or a universal reminder that the best of who we are can emerge and define us when encouraged and nurtured by family. And yet Gerwig’s adaptation makes clear that while the bars of sunlight beam throughout the March house with raw energy and unabashed happiness, the world still intrudes. Life happens. Events must be sorted out. The March women anxiously await the safe return of the father, gone to fight in the Civil War. Their gentle and raucous chatter, the sheer vitality of these little women, represents a hybrid of modern consciousness as well as an acceptance of the decorum and social constraints of their time, made especially concrete by Meg and Amy. Don’t miss this film. It’s worth seeing on the big screen. In so many ways, it is larger than life. Little Women. Written and directed by Greta Gerwig. articles.text: Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a day care center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat-of-your-pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a coming of age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes and Toy Story 3 may turn out to be the sweetest and best-told story of the summer. Toy Story 3 (Animation). Starring the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Rated PG.

articles.text: A town hall style meeting was convened on June 29 via Zoom by Berkeley Symphony in collaboration with the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco. Ref lections Town Hall, a panel discussion on social justice co-presented by The Commonwealth Club of California and Berkeley Symphony, took place through Zoom technology on Monday, June 29. The town hall-type gathering convened a panel of thought leaders to examine the role of arts organizations in addressing racial injustice. The discussion included Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young, Dr. Deborah L. Gould, Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan, educator Charles McNeal, Cal Performances Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen, and Jeff Benson, Executive Director of SWAG Foundation. The discussion was organized by Berkeley Symphony Board President Shariq Yosufzai, with Joseph Young serving as moderator. “I’m always reminded to remember that the fight for social justice is no sprint. The work that institutions must do to demolish centuries of systemic racism will still take years, and even decades of individual reflection and action,” Young said, before introducing the panel of thought leaders. The panel convened a few weeks after the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, and subsequent protests nationwide and worldwide. Young began the discussion with a question to the panelists: “Why do you think there is such a big reaction now from whites, blacks, and even arts organizations about police brutality?” Morgan opened by pointing to the current health crisis and shelter-in-place regulations. “The single upside of the COVID crisis, is that everyone is home and is able to focus on what’s going on in the world. None of this is new; we’ve always been so busy where we can sort of look away and keep going on with our lives,” Morgan said. Morgan observed that the young protestors are “the real heroes right now, taking up the torch.” “I feel like this modern movement was really sparked by Trayvon Martin, because that was where the catalyst began, where we began to see a crystal-clear element of racial divide and racism,” noted Charles McNeal, San Francisco Opera’s Director of Diversity. “We have environmental distress, political distress, we have an education system in shreds. The wound has been opened.” McNeal agreed that COVID- 19, and regulations related to it, helped fuel the nationwide discussion surrounding racial equity. “We’ve all been devastated by [COVID-19], and that was an awakening of the integral nature of things, we’re all connected. Your freedom is my freedom, and your pain is my pain,” he said. Young asked the panel for suggestions on how organizations can be held accountable for their social impact. McNeal said that organizations should be “engaged learning organizations,” implementing ongoing, sustainable plan in approaching this complex issue. “If you do not change, you become extinct,” Dr. Gould added, referencing Spencer Johnson’s Who Moved My Cheese? “Listening with humility, and working to transform requires trust and a culture where everyone feels valued,” she said. The town hall concluded with a song from the Oakland Interfaith Community Choir. “As a message of standing together, and of Black Lives Matter, the choir published a video titled ‘Hear my Prayer.’ As we all reflect, even as we can’t come together as artists, we still sing,” Young said. You can view the panel discussion on Youtube at https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=0IMN_ XFT1WE&feature=youtu.be. articles.text: There are many social issues hitting us in the face these days. Whether it’s pretense or poverty, we find ourselves on the ropes. Music can do more than soothe the savage beast… much more. Throughout history, those who aspired to upward mobility utilized a number of stratagems. Sports comes to mind first. Just think of the many sports heroes who rose to fame and inspired all of us. The Irish can claim John L Sullivan; and many others of ALL ethnicities followed him in the boxing ring. Joe Louis was honored by President Franklin Roosevelt as an honor to the human race. What an inspiration he was! Likewise, the Latin-Americans and the Asians. Jews also fought their way out of the ghetto via the boxing ring. But they also did it in the concert halls. The instrument of choice most often was the violin. As a people, they were kept in poverty. Pianos were expensive but violins were cheap. Pianos were also big and heavy. So, if you got expelled from your town or from your country you couldn’t move easily with the monster piano. But you could with a small violin. The violin was also an expression of an entire peoples‘ emotional outcry. Do these things sound familiar? Do these issues really change? Music was also a financial passport out of misery. But other factors played a big part. Music, you see, has many contradictions. In the first place it teaches literacy. Education is the first step forward. But at the same time the language of music is both specific and merely suggestive. In other words, you must follow directions and at the same time you must think for yourself. A musician must practice alone in order to be expressive and emotional in public. How about that for a contradiction! Music teaches us to be, at the very same time, a team player and a self-centered star. Music does not know the prejudice of age nor the prejudice of religion nor the prejudice of ethnicity or the prejudice of sexual orientation. Oh sure, there have been a few bad apples. But their numbers are so small when compared to those who can see beyond the horizon. A perfect example of this is the generous former conductor of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, Edgar Braun. He was made administrator of a government- sponsored orchestra back in the 1970s. The government bureaucrat who was in charge wanted to establish quotas for the players. Edgar told me that he hired one black player. The government administrator said: “the quota of black players has now been set at one.“ Not long after this, Edgar hired another black player. The government administrator phoned Edgar saying: “You are in violation of your quota. Your quota is one black player and you now have two.“ Edgar, thinking very fast replied: “I don’t know how to tell you this, Sir, but my ears are colorblind.” There was silence at the other end of the phone. The bureaucrat did not know what to say. After a little while he said: “OK.” That was the end of it. I wonder if the bureaucrat learned anything. The great Greek philosopher Aristotle had a lot to say on the importance of music. In fact, the ancient Greeks advocated that music was the equal to mathematics/science and sports. Those were the three most important subjects during the golden age of Greece. Where will we find another Aristotle to enlighten those who need enlightenment? I am sure that Aristotle could say it simple enough even for those folks to understand. “Music has proven its worth in society. What we need is more music… especially in our schools.” NEXT WEEK: Famous temper tantrums in the world of music.

articles.text: Jon Sigurdson, a resident of Piedmont since 1970, passed away at home with his family on June 16, 2020. He was 86. Born Jon Frederick Page Sigurdson in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada on July 2, 1933, he was the third child of Larus Arthur and Helen Page Sigurdson. After completing his Bachelor of Arts at the University of Manitoba, Jon followed in his father’s footsteps by studying medicine. In 1959 he received his Doctor of Medicine from the University of Manitoba with an emphasis in Anatomy and Physiology. While in medical school, Jon met the love of his life, Margaret Jean Watson. They were married on July 19, 1958. After completing his internship at Winnipeg General Hospital, Jon and Margaret moved to Philadelphia in 1960 for his orthopedic residency at the University of Pennsylvania. While in Philadelphia, their only child, Helen Margaret Jean, was born. In 1964, the family moved to Oakland, CA where Jon joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group. In 1970, Jon went into solo private practice in Oakland with Margaret as his office manager. Jon was very active in the orthopedic community and served on the Board of Councilors of the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons from 1983 to 1989. He enjoyed a successful orthopedic practice and retired in 2011. Jon was a passionate student of the arts. He received a Music degree as a Piano Solo Performer from the Royal Conservatory of Music of Toronto in 1956. His love of music led Jon and Margaret to be long time patrons of the San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Opera. His memberships in the Canadian and the British Orthopedic communities led them to medical meetings and an opportunity to meet new friends all over the world. Jon enjoyed studying art, history and geography. Together, he and Margaret took classes at the De Young Museum and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. As voracious readers, they were long-time members of two book clubs. Jon and Margaret were also avid hikers. They hiked the West Highland Way in Scotland, the full length of the Thames, and the Milford Track in Australia. He delighted in taking his family to historical sites throughout the U.S., Canada and Europe. Jon was a devoted, husband, father and grandfather. He passed his love of arts and outdoors to his daughter and granddaughters. Jon was an active member of the First Presbyterian Church of Oakland for over 50 years and was instrumental in the installation of the church organ. He was also a member of the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, the Oakland Rotary Club and the Grandfathers’ Club. As a member of the Home Club, he and Margaret enjoyed ballroom dancing with friends. Jon is survived by his wife Jon Sigurdson, who lived in Piedmont for 50 years, passed away on June 16. He was 86. Margaret, his daughter Helen Sigurdson Hayes, his granddaughters Lara Jean Hayes and Liana Ann Hayes and many nieces and nephews. He is predeceased by his sister, Frances Giddings, of Anchorage, AK, and brothers Johannes Arthur of Winnipeg, MB and Eric Lawrence of Ottawa, ON. A Memorial service will be held at the Chapel of the Chimes in Oakland on Friday, July 17 at 11 a.m. He was buried at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. The family requests that in lieu of flowers, memorial donations in the name of Jon Sigurdson be made to Meals on Wheels, the Salvation Army or in support of the Arts. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 8, 2020 By T.J. Stevko When facing illness, take control of finances In light of the coronavirus pandemic, virtually all of us have considered health-related issues. But for people facing a serious, chronic illness, such as Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, diabetes or cancer, health concerns are an everyday matter. If you’re fortunate, you may never be afflicted with such maladies, but the future is unpredictable. Of course, going through these health challenges bring physical and emotional concerns – but also financial ones. How can you prepare for them? Essentially, you’ll need to consider four key areas: investments, insurance, legal arrangements and taxes. Let’s take a quick look at each of them: • Investments You’ll likely need to draw on your investments for at least some of the expenses associated with your illness. So, within your portfolio, you may want to establish a special fund devoted entirely to these costs, whether they be health care, modifications to your home, transportation and so on. A financial professional can help you choose investments for this fund, as well as make recommendations for your overall investment strategy, including techniques for boosting your income, such as adding investments that can provide an income stream that kicks in when you think your costs will rise. • Insurance Depending on your health status, you may be able to collect Medicare earlier than the traditional starting point at age 65. Even so, you’ll likely need to supplement it with additional coverage. But you may also want to look beyond health insurance. For example, you might be able to purchase a “chronic illness rider” that allows you to tap into life insurance benefits while you’re still alive. Or you might consider adding a “long-term care rider” to a life insurance policy; this rider offers financial benefits if you ever require daily care that you can’t provide for yourself. And some foundations, states and drug companies offer programs that can help pay for some costs that your insurance won’t cover. • Legal arrangements If you haven’t already done so, you may want to establish the legal documents most appropriate for your situation, such as a durable power of attorney for finances, which gives someone the authority to manage your financial affairs if you become temporarily incapacitated, possibly due to flare-ups of your chronic disease. Once you’ve recovered, you regain control of your financial decisions. You might also want to consider a health care proxy, which appoints an individual to make medical decisions for you if you can’t. In creating or revising these documents, you’ll need to consult with your legal professional. • Taxes You might qualify for Social Security disability payments, which, like other Social Security benefits, are taxable, so you’ll need to be aware of what you might owe. But you might also be eligible for some tax breaks related to your condition. If you still itemize tax deductions, you may be able to deduct some medical expenses, as well as certain home improvements, such as wheelchair ramps, bathtub grab bars, motorized stairlifts and so on. Your tax advisor may have suggestions appropriate for your situation. Dealing with a chronic illness is never easy. But by considering how your illness will affect all aspects of your life, getting the help you need, and taking the right steps, you may be able to reduce the financial stress on you and your loved ones. articles.text: Piedmont needs to decrease emissions another 13.5% by 2030 to meet CAP goals Greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont have decreased in recent years, according to a report presented by Justin Szasz, Climate Fellow, to City Council on Monday, July 6. The report was an inventory of greenhouse gases emitted in 2018 and found that total emissions were down over 26 percent compared to 2005. In 2018, the City estimates there were 34,340 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, compared to 48,818 metric tons in 2005 and 38,101 metric tons in 2017. The report noted 934 metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018 were attributed to activities done by the City government. In the past 15 years, greenhouse gas emissions have dropped mostly due to a reduction in appliance use. “The reductions since 2005 are largely due to decreases in emissions from building appliances,” the report explained. Piedmonters appear to be using less natural gas appliances at home. The report notes the increased use of electric utility systems appears to have contributed to the decrease. However, much of the decreased use of appliances can be ascribed to the fact that winters have been warmer in recent years, a trend that scientists blame on global warming. Although reported emissions decreased almost 10 percent from 2017 to 2018, the City attributed this decline to changes in methodology. In fact, the City believes did not change significantly in this time period. “Reductions between 2017 and 2018, by contrast, are largely attributable to changes in in the protocols for estimating emissions, not to emission reductions happening in Piedmont,” the report said. The inventory suggests that the report for 2019 emissions will show a notable decrease, though, because the City has enrolled in an electricity plan that powers Piedmont with 100 percent renewable energy. This action was part of the Climate Action Plan (CAP) adopted by the City in 2018. While the amount of emissions from appliances decreased, emissions from vehicles have held steady from 2015 to 2018. The CAP goals adopted in 2018 push Piedmont to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 40 percent below 2005 levels by 2030. By 2050, the CAP sets forth the goal of reducing emissions to 80 percent below 2005. The inventory released this week shows that Piedmont still has some work to do in order to reach its goals in 10 years. “The inventories completed thus far reveal that, for the most part, the changes from year to year are caused by external forces, and that the City still has a long way to go to make substantive changes to the building energy sector and the transportation sector so that it can meet the City’s 2030 and 2050 goals,” the report said. The City must reduce 2018 emission levels another 13.5 percent in order to reach the CAP goals by 2030.

See it filled with your own objects and art. Visualize that the space is clean and clutter-free. Next, ask yourself, what do I want for this room? And notice what arises. Do you imagine rearranging it? Are you willing to let go of certain pieces? Are there items in that room that you’ve been telling yourself a story about, justifying why you should hang onto it? Whatever new ideas come to you in this vision, when you are ready, open your eyes and make some notes. This is you, creating your own vision for the home that will support you in becoming your best self. Do you share your home with a partner, with family? Have everyone try this exercise. Have them envision the same space, or their own spaces. See what everyone comes up with. Thought becomes form. If we can dream it, we can create it. But without a clear sense of our own vision, we might find ourselves just grabbing whatever looks good at the retail furniture outlet or being swayed by the marketing story on page 34 of a print catalog. Maybe you don’t want to sit and do vision work. If that is the case, try this: Simply notice the energy that you’re in when you are thinking about making a change to your home. Is it the energy of, “I want my home to look good because I care what other people think,” or is it, “I want it to feel good so that I will be able to be more connected to myself”? Which of these thoughts is more inspiring for you? Adjust your inner monologue as needed. Another way that we can create a more connected environment is to be visioning when we are in an energy-rich state. So, be very mindful about how you are feeling when you are looking for things for your home. Try this: Meditate (if that is your jam) or go for a walk in nature before going online to shop for furnishings. articles.text: In time-honored tradition, the Piedmont 4th of July Parade Committee toured the city the nigh before the parade to observe locations of all parade entries. With the cancellation of the parade due to concerns of COVID-19, there were no floats this year. Instead, with a theme of Celebrating in Place, residents submitted entry forms describing the decorations on their homes and cars. After viewing the 20 entries, the committee is presenting the following awards: Highland Cup Best Entry: Mason & Austin Gray, 23 Piedmont Court, “Bloom Where You Are Planted” (2nd generation owners) All decorations were created by sons Mason & Austin, including a large sign on the garage reading ”Don’t forget true beauty.” Highland Saucer Most Patriotic: Barbara Addelman, 225 Carmel Ave., “This is What Democracy Looks Like” Large collection of handmade signs from historic civic protests in the U.S, going back to the rallies by Native Americans at Standing Rock, North Dakota. Highland Spoons Best Quaranteam: Buffy Yeh & Neighbors, 223 Park View Ave, “Celebrating with Patriotism and Protests” Mayor’s Award “E Pluribus Unum – Out of Many, One”, Julia Elitzer, 128 Greenbank Ave. Handmade flags of every state in the U.S., and a dozen countries outside the U.S. Best Car in Place Rod Boothby, 1132 Oakland Ave. Most Artistic Award “Pollinator Posse,” Terry Smith, 121 Fairview As a science teacher, the display calls attention to importance of creating pollinator-friendly gardens. Best Spirit Award “Do the Right Thing”, Sydney Proctor and Team Proctor, 385 Moraga Ave. A collection of signs promoting racial justice, include Black Lives Matter.

articles.text: At 8:12 a.m. on Thursday morning, July 2, the Piedmont Police received a call about an attempted robbery, attempted stolen vehicle and death threat by a person with a knife and in possession of burglary tools. A contractor hired to paint the inside of a Piedmont home went outside to his vehicle and saw a man inside his vehicle. The contractor chased the suspect down Highland Ave. The suspect then turned around and brandished an 8-10” black knife toward the contractor, who immediately ran back away from the suspect. The suspect then chased the contractor. When the contractor fell to the ground, the suspect demanded the contractor’s wallet. The contractor refused and the suspect was unable to take any property from him or his vehicle. The suspect then fled in a grey Toyota Camry southbound on Highland Ave. The suspect’s vehicle had been stolen from Fairfield. Police issued a BOLO (Be on the lookout for) alert notice to other jurisdictions.

Roland Lazzorotto, the official Parade Starter wearing a tuxedo, favored the innovative decorating efforts that included awareness of social injustice. “I know that we have a pretty educated and sophisticated community here. Nevertheless, I was pleasantly surprised to see the outpouring of support for Black Lives Matter throughout town. It is nice when you can be proud of your neighbors and your town.” One modest entry provided a much-needed respite for some of the judges at Colleen Gallagher’s home on Oakland Avenue where she provided a Lemonade Stand just for the Fourth. One of the best entries was saved for last. Barbara Addelman and family on Carmel Avenue set up a yard filled with handmade signs based upon the theme, “This is What Democracy Looks Like”. The impressive assemblage of included historic civic protests in the U.S, going back to the rallies by Native Americans at Standing Rock in North Dakota. Signs for social causes filled up dozens of small windows out front and cutout protesters held up pickets. Signs read “Black Lives Matter,” “Water is Life,” “Google: Fred Hampton,” “We Stand with Hong Hong,” and dozens more. This installation and fan favorite won the Highland Saucer for Most Patriotic entry. In the end, the first ever Celebrate in Place immobile parade contest succeeded in bringing dozens of households and neighbors together to get creative, patriotic and crafty. Chair of the Parade Committee Carla Betts gave her stamp of approval. “I enjoyed the diversity, dedication, and the spirit of the entrants. As a committee member, it was a special day in Piedmont,” she said. The Addelman-Cumming family theme was “This is What Democracy Looks Like”, with a plethora of protest signs such as “Who Watches the Watchers,” “Freedom of the Press,” and “Racism isn’t getting worse, it’s getting filmed.” CRIME REPORT Attempted robbery, car theft by suspect with knife By Jay Russell At 8:12 a.m. on Thursday morning, July 2, the Piedmont Police received a call about an attempted robbery, attempted stolen vehicle and death threat by a person with a knife and in possession of burglary tools.
